program_name: Languages and Literatures for European Plurilingualism — official Italian degree title: "Corso di Studio Magistrale in Lingue e Letterature per il Plurilinguismo Europeo" (CdSM). Unlike the Economics and Finance (LMEF) programme, whose diploma name is itself in English, THE LEGAL DIPLOMA NAME OF THIS COURSE IS ITALIAN: the degree awarded is "Dottore Magistrale in Lingue e letterature per il Plurilinguismo europeo", and "Languages and Literatures for European Plurilingualism" is the official English rendering used on the orientation portal, the international course catalogue and the University's own English-language edition of the didactic regulations. This is a standalone programme, NOT a curriculum inside a larger Italian-taught degree, and it is formally recognised as a course "with an international character" pursuant to Ministerial Decree 6/2019 (Annex A, Table K) — the orientation portal states this explicitly: "The international (M.D. 6/2019, Annex A, Table K) Master's Degree Course in LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES FOR EUROPEAN PLURILINGUALISM". Offered by the Department of Humanities (Dipartimento di Studi Umanistici — DSU), School of Human and Social Sciences (Scuola delle Scienze Umane e Sociali), teaching area "Studi Umanistici". Two years, 120 CFU. Internal University course code: P60 (used in the file names and headers of the official didactic regulations, e.g. "P60 DSU Regulation CdSM Languages and Literatures for European Multilingualism") — but the department's own course landing page prints "(P61)" instead; see uncertainty_notes. The course is subdivided into curricula (four per the orientation portal and the regulations, five per the departmental detail page — see uncertainty_notes): LINGUISTIC (LIN), LITERARY-HISTORICAL (SLE), BINATIONAL LITERARY-HISTORICAL "Cultura e Letteratura in Europa / Kultur und Literatur in Europa" (A33), LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES FOR TEACHERS (LLD), and BINATIONAL LINGUISTIC "Didattica del FLE". NOTE ON THE ENGLISH NAME: official University sources are internally inconsistent, rendering the title with both "Plurilingualism" and "Multilingualism" — the English edition of the didactic regulations is headed "LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES FOR EUROPEAN PLURILINGUALISM" but its own page footer reads "CdSM Languages and Literatures for European Multilingualism", and the orientation portal's double-degree paragraph switches to "LANGUAGES AND LITERATURE FOR EUROPEAN MULTILINGUALISM". "Plurilingualism" is the form used in the page titles, the international course catalogue and the URL slug, and is treated here as the official English name.
level: master (Italian "Laurea Magistrale", second-cycle degree, 2 years, 120 CFU). Official wording: "Tipo di corso: Magistrale" / "Durata: 2 anni"; orientation portal header "Master's Degree"; "Degree required Laurea I Livello" (a first-cycle/bachelor's degree is required for entry). Credit structure published for every curriculum on the orientation portal is identical in shape: 1st year 66 CFU + 2nd year 54 CFU = 120 CFU, invariably including "Training and internship (150 hours) – 6 cfu" and "Final Paper – 12 cfu" in the second year. The internship is compulsory: the regulations state "Traineeship and internship are compulsory and contribute to the award of credits for the other training activities". Each CFU corresponds to 25 hours of total student workload, with 5 contact hours per CFU for lectures; language teaching additionally carries "language exercises for a total of 96 additional hours per year" delivered by the University Language Centre (CLA) mother-tongue language experts. Graduates hold the title "Dottore Magistrale".
teaching_language:
[uncertain] ENGLISH IS OFFERED AS A COMPLETE PATHWAY, BUT THIS IS A PLURILINGUAL COURSE, NOT A CONVENTIONAL ENGLISH-MEDIUM DEGREE — and this distinction is the single most important thing to understand about the programme. Do not read the "ENG" tag as equivalent to the fully English-taught degrees elsewhere at Federico II.

WHAT THE OFFICIAL SOURCES SAY. (a) The orientation portal course-sheet header records "Language ENG" — a single ENG tag with no ITA component, the same tag format used for Federico II's fully English-taught degrees. (b) The international course catalogue lists the entry under Humanities as "Languages and Literatures for European Plurilingualism – ENG". (c) But the binding didactic regulations and the departmental course page both describe a conditional, student-elected arrangement rather than a uniform English medium: "The last, but fundamental, aspect to be highlighted with regard to the training activities offered by the CdSM with a view to multilingualism is the possibility for students to carry out their entire course of study in English or, for the other foreign languages and literatures, in the relevant languages and in English. In this way, the CdSM intends to meet the qualification of a Course of Study with an international character pursuant to Ministerial Decree 6/2019 (Annex A, Table K)." The Italian original is equally conditional: "offre infine la possibilità che gli studenti possano svolgere l'intero percorso di studi in lingua inglese oppure, per gli insegnamenti delle altre lingue e letterature straniere, nelle relative lingue e in inglese."

HOW TO READ THIS. English is the language in which a student MAY elect to complete the whole degree; it is the vehicle that earns the course its "international character" qualification under M.D. 6/2019. It is not the sole language of instruction. By design the curriculum is delivered across French, Spanish, English, German and Italian: teaching of each foreign language and literature takes place in that language and/or in English, and the published study plans contain modules that are inherently Italian-medium — "Italian Linguistics", "Italian literature", "Modern and Contemporary Italian Literature", "History of the Latin Language", "Medieval and Humanistic Latin Literature", "Latin teaching", "Teaching History of Philosophy", "General and Social Pedagogy", "Dynamic Psychology". The Linguistic curriculum makes "Italian Linguistics – 6 cfu" a compulsory second-year module, and the Languages and Literatures for Teachers curriculum requires "One course to choose from: Italian literature or Italian Linguistics – 6 cfu". Language practice classes are run "by language experts from the University Language Centre for each of the languages offered".

CORROBORATING SIGNALS THAT THIS IS A MULTI-LANGUAGE COURSE. The didactic regulations are officially published in FOUR languages — Italian, English, French and German ("Versione inglese", "Versione francesce" [sic], "Versione tedesca") — which no single-language English-medium programme at Federico II does. The thesis rule is explicitly not English-bound: "The thesis, no less than 100 pages long, must be written in Italian or in one of the foreign languages studied during the two-year course... Part of the discussion will be held in a foreign language." And the international course catalogue records the Bordeaux-Montaigne binational double degree under this same programme as "LANGUAGE: ITA/FRA" — Italian/French, with no English at all — so at least one published pathway of this degree is not English-medium in any part.

Marked uncertain because no unina.it source publishes a module-by-module language map, states which modules are guaranteed to run in English in a given year, or confirms that an English-only route is actually timetabled and viable every year for a student with no Italian. The regulations promise the "possibility"; the operational guarantee is not documented. A candidate who cannot follow Italian must confirm the point directly with the coordinator (luca.zenobi@unina.it) before applying — particularly given that the same regulations require B2 Italian at entry (see language_requirements).

degree_class: LM-37 — Italian degree class LM-37 "Lingue e letterature moderne europee e americane" (Modern European and American Languages and Literatures). Stated identically across all official sources: the orientation portal header ("Degree class LM-37"), the departmental detail sheet ("Classi di Laurea: LM-37 Classe delle lauree magistrali in Lingue e letterature moderne europee e americane"), and the cover page of the official didactic regulations ("LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES FOR EUROPEAN PLURILINGUALISM — CLASS LM-37"), whose Art. 1 repeats: "These Regulations govern the organisational aspects of the Master's Degree Course in LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES FOR EUROPEAN PLURILINGUSLISM (class LM-37)" [sic — typographical error in the official English text]. This confirms the degree_class given in the research brief.
admission_type:
OPEN ACCESS (Italian "accesso libero") WITH COMPULSORY CURRICULAR SCREENING AND A DISCRETIONARY ASSESSMENT OF PERSONAL PREPARATION. The orientation portal course-sheet header records "Admission Libero" (free/open) and "Degree required Laurea I Livello". "Libero" means there is NO numerus clausus, NO ranked competition against other candidates, NO published seat cap, and consequently NO rectoral admission decree (bando) of the kind published for Medicine, Architecture or the locally capped bachelor's courses.

HOWEVER, open access does NOT mean automatic admission, and the gate here is unusually demanding on paper. Two things are verified before enrolment: (1) SPECIFIC CURRICULAR REQUIREMENTS — the applicant must hold a bachelor's degree in one of the listed classes AND have accumulated 48 CFU in two foreign-language sectors plus 48 CFU in two foreign-literature sectors (see academic_requirements); (2) THE ADEQUACY OF PERSONAL PREPARATION — assessed case by case. The regulations (Art. 5 §2) state: "In addition to the possession of specific curricular requirements, admission to the CdSM is subject to verification of the adequacy of the student's personal preparation. As provided for in the CdSM regulations, the Teaching Coordination Commission assesses the personal suitability of applicants on a case-by-case basis. It reserves the right to carry out written tests and personal interviews, also through special committees."

CRITICALLY, THE CURRICULAR SHORTFALL RULE IS STRICT AND HAS NO CONDITIONAL/OFA ROUTE: "Students who do not meet the above-mentioned requirements may only be admitted to the Master's Degree Course after having acquired the relevant credits." That is, missing credits must be made good BEFORE admission (typically by enrolling in single courses — "corsi singoli" — under the University's separate regulations, for which the CCD may recognise up to 36 CFU); they cannot be carried into the degree as additional obligations. This is materially harsher than the LMEF economics model, where shortfall candidates are simply examined at interview.

ONE AUTOMATIC-ENTRY CASE IS DEFINED: "A Bachelor's degree in Class L-11 (Modern Languages and Cultures) from the Faculty of Arts and Philosophy (or the Department of Humanities) of the University of Naples Federico II... allows enrolment in the Master's Degree Course... without any credits to be acquired." In-house Federico II L-11 graduates therefore bypass the credit check entirely.

NOT TOLC-based; NOT SAT-based; NOT a selection call (bando di selezione); no standing written entrance examination; no GRE/GMAT requirement published anywhere on unina.it. NOTE: the internal selections for the binational/double-degree tracks (Osnabrück, Bordeaux-Montaigne) ARE competitive and ranked, but they take place DURING the first year among already-enrolled students — they are not an admission route into the degree (see seats_total).
academic_requirements:
[uncertain] ENTRY QUALIFICATION — A CLOSED LIST OF BACHELOR'S DEGREE CLASSES. The didactic regulations (Art. 4) require a Bachelor's Degree obtained in one of the following classes under Ministerial Decree 509/1999: "11 Modern Languages and Cultures; 03 Language Mediation Sciences; 05 Humanities"; or, under Ministerial Decree 270/2004: "L-11 Modern languages and cultures; L-10 Humanities; L-12 Language Mediation." (The two decrees are successive Italian regulatory frameworks; 11/03/05 are the older codes and L-11/L-12/L-10 the current equivalents, so in practice this is one list of three subject areas: modern languages and cultures, language mediation, and humanities.) The orientation portal publishes the same list. NOTE A WORDING DEFECT: the English regulations join the two decree lists with "as well as" ("in one of the following degree classes provided for by Ministerial Decree 509/1999... as well as in one of the following degree classes envisaged by Ministerial Decree 270/2004"), which read literally would require a degree under BOTH decrees — an impossibility. The orientation portal's "or in one of the following classes" is the correct reading; see uncertainty_notes.

CURRICULAR CREDIT REQUIREMENTS — THE DECISIVE AND VERY HEAVY BARRIER. Beyond the degree class, the applicant must ALSO have obtained, during the bachelor's: "a minimum number of 48 CFU within two of the following disciplines: L-LIN/04 French Language; L-LIN/07 Spanish Language; L-LIN/12 English Language; L-LIN/14 German Language" AND "48 CFU within two of the following disciplines: L-LIN/03 French Literature; L-LIN/05 Spanish Literature; L-LIN/10 English Literature; L-LIN/13 German Literature." That is 96 CFU in total — 48 in two foreign LANGUAGES and a further 48 in two foreign LITERATURES — out of a 180-CFU Italian bachelor, i.e. well over half the degree must consist of foreign language and literature coursework in exactly these Italian scientific-disciplinary sectors (SSD). This is the single hardest requirement in the record and is calibrated to an Italian L-11/L-12 languages bachelor. Two languages are required, not one: a candidate with a deep single-language background (e.g. English only) does not satisfy it.

SHORTFALL RULE — NO CONDITIONAL ADMISSION: "Students who do not meet the above-mentioned requirements may only be admitted to the Master's Degree Course after having acquired the relevant credits." Missing credits must be earned before admission, not remediated afterwards.

EXEMPTION: "A Bachelor's degree in Class L-11 (Modern Languages and Cultures) from the Faculty of Arts and Philosophy (or the Department of Humanities) of the University of Naples Federico II, either according to the system defined by Ministerial Decree 509/1999 or according to the system defined by Ministerial Decree 270/2004, allows enrolment in the Master's Degree Course... without any credits to be acquired."

PERSONAL PREPARATION: assessed case by case by the Didactic Coordination Commission (CCD), which "reserves the right to carry out written tests and personal interviews, also through special committees."

FOREIGN APPLICANTS. The regulations address them only procedurally, not substantively: the CCD "examines and evaluates... enrolment received from students holding degrees obtained at foreign universities" and "recognition of studies completed at foreign universities in accordance with the procedures set out in Article 16 of the RDA, and decides on their approval". Separately, for language: "For students who have obtained a degree from foreign universities, the Commission for the Didactic Coordination of the Master's Degree Course shall assess on a case-by-case basis the possession of the minimum level of knowledge of the Italian language." Holders of foreign qualifications must additionally satisfy the University's central recognition rules (translations, legalisation, Diploma Supplement, examination certificates, CIMEA/ENIC-NARIC comparability statement, Declaration of Value).

Marked uncertain for the reason that matters most to an international candidate: NO unina.it source explains how the 48+48 CFU requirement is mapped onto a non-Italian bachelor's transcript, which carries no L-LIN/xx SSD codes at all. Whether a foreign languages degree is assessed by equivalent content, by ECTS volume, or by some conversion is nowhere stated, and the outcome rests entirely with the CCD. Unlike LMEF, whose sources say explicitly that "for foreign applicants credits' fulfilment will be individually determined by the Master's admission committee", no comparable relieving statement exists here — the regulations state the 48+48 rule without any published foreign-degree carve-out. An international applicant must obtain a written case-by-case ruling from the coordinator before relying on eligibility.
language_requirements:
[uncertain] THIS IS THE DECISIVE FIELD FOR INTERNATIONAL CANDIDATES, AND IT CONTAINS A DIRECT CONFLICT BETWEEN THE PROGRAMME'S OWN REGULATIONS AND THE UNIVERSITY'S CENTRAL RULE.

WHAT THE PROGRAMME'S BINDING REGULATION REQUIRES — B2 IN EVERY LANGUAGE, INCLUDING ITALIAN. Didactic Regulations, Art. 4 §2, verbatim: "The minimum entry level required in each language, including Italian, is B2 of the Common European Framework (CEFR). This level is considered to have been reached with the possession of the 48 CFU in the foreign language sectors indicated above as an entry requirement, and as regards the Italian language with the possession of one of the three-year degrees among those indicated above as an entry requirement. For students who have obtained a degree from foreign universities, the Commission for the Didactic Coordination of the Master's Degree Course shall assess on a case-by-case basis the possession of the minimum level of knowledge of the Italian language."

Unpacking this: (i) CEFR B2 is required in EACH language the student will work in AND in ITALIAN; (ii) for Italian applicants both are deemed satisfied automatically — the foreign-language B2 by the 48 CFU, and the Italian B2 by holding one of the listed Italian bachelor's degrees; (iii) FOR FOREIGN-DEGREE HOLDERS NEITHER DEEMING RULE APPLIES AUTOMATICALLY, and the CCD assesses Italian proficiency case by case. In other words, an applicant with a non-Italian bachelor faces an explicit, individually adjudicated ITALIAN-LANGUAGE requirement at B2 — on a course tagged "ENG".

THE CONFLICT WITH THE CENTRAL RULE. international.unina.it states: "If you choose a three-year, five-year or single-cycle degree course in ENGLISH, level B2 Italian language proficiency is not required." On its face that waiver would exempt candidates to this English-tagged course. But two things undercut a confident reliance on it: (a) the waiver clause enumerates "three-year, five-year or single-cycle" courses and conspicuously does NOT list magistrale (master's) courses, whereas the parallel clause imposing the requirement DOES enumerate them — "If you choose a three-year degree course, magistral degree course or single-cycle magistral degree course in ITALIAN, a B2 level Italian language proficiency is required"; (b) even if the central waiver applies, it governs the visa/pre-enrolment administrative gate, whereas Art. 4 §2 is the course's own academic admission rule, and the two operate independently. The safe working assumption for this programme is that Italian will be assessed.

ENGLISH. Required in substance but with NO published threshold of its own and NO list of accepted certificates. English enters the requirement only as one of the languages caught by the general "B2 in each language" rule, and only if the student elects English as one of their two languages (English is one of four options — French, Spanish, English, German — and is not compulsory). No IELTS/TOEFL/Cambridge score table exists on any unina.it page for this course. For an Italian applicant, English proficiency is deemed proven by the L-LIN/12 credits inside the 48 CFU language block.

A FURTHER LANGUAGE GATE — THE BINATIONAL TRACKS. Students selected for the Osnabrück track need German: "UNINA students are required to have a level of competence in German equal to at least level B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages." For the Bordeaux-Montaigne track: "having a B2 level of knowledge of the language of the University where they will be accepted" (i.e. French). These apply to the in-course selection, not to admission.

DEGREE-EXIT EXPECTATION. The regulations set the training target above entry level: the specialisation pathway aims "in at least one European adoptive language and literature" at "a truly advanced level of competence... (cf. levels C of competence in the CEFR)" — i.e. C1/C2 by graduation.

VISA CAVEAT: the central regulation adds that "an international certificate attesting to the level of English language skills (IELTS, TOEFL, Cambridge, etc.) is useful for the issue of the visa by the diplomatic/consular Representation", so a non-EU applicant should hold one regardless.

Marked uncertain because: no CEFR certificate list, exemption route or test procedure is published for this course; the Italian B2 rule for foreign-degree holders is expressly left to case-by-case CCD judgement with no stated evidence standard; and the central English-course waiver and Art. 4 §2 point in opposite directions with no unina.it page reconciling them. Prospective international applicants must resolve this in writing with the coordinator (luca.zenobi@unina.it) and international.ma.plurilingualism@gmail.com before committing.
application_deadline_eu:
[uncertain] NO PROGRAMME-SPECIFIC APPLICATION DEADLINE IS PUBLISHED ON ANY unina.it PAGE for this course, for 2026/2027 or for any other year. This programme is open access, so there is no bando with a dated application window of the kind capped courses publish; admission runs as an individual eligibility assessment by the coordinator/CCD followed by ordinary matriculation.

WHAT IS PUBLISHED. The orientation portal gives only the University's standard matriculation window, and with an important qualifier: "Registration and enrolment to years following the first one normally take place between 1 September and 31 October each year, in accordance with the procedures that are published in a specific Guide to Enrolment and Fee Payment at: https://www.unina.it/didattica/sportello-studenti/guide-dello-studente. Further deadlines can be found on the website of the Department of Humanities: https://www.studiumanistici.unina.it". Note that this sentence is expressly about "years following the first one" — it does not state the first-year enrolment window, and the portal gives no separate first-year date.

ROUTE FOR EU CANDIDATES HOLDING A FOREIGN QUALIFICATION (deadline-free, centrally defined): "If you are an italian candidate or a candidate from the European Union wherever you reside and regularly residing in Italy or in a European Union country have unrestricted access to university courses if you hold a foreign qualification corresponding to the required Italian qualification. In this case you have to send your academic documents to the Coordinator of the course you wish to enrol in to find out whether you meet the enrolment requirements." No calendar deadline attaches to this coordinator-assessment step; in practice it must precede matriculation, and the CCD's case-by-case assessment of curricular credits and Italian proficiency should be started months ahead.

RELATED DATES THAT ARE PUBLISHED (academic calendar for 2026/2027, approved by the Department Council on 28 May 2026): teaching runs "I Semestre: dal 1° ottobre" — first semester from 1 October 2026. The orientation portal describes the general shape: "The teaching calendar is divided into two semesters of lessons (October-December and March-May) and three ordinary examination sessions (January-February, June-July, September) alongside two extra sessions (April and November)."

Marked uncertain because no first-year application or enrolment deadline for this programme exists anywhere on unina.it; the only published window explicitly concerns continuing students; and the department's own notice board carries no 2026/27 admission timetable for the course. An EU applicant must obtain the operative date from segreteria/coordinator rather than infer it.
application_deadline_non_eu:
[uncertain] AND TIME-CRITICAL. Non-EU candidates residing abroad face stacked deadlines, and the binding one for this open-access course has almost certainly already passed as of the research date (2026-08-30).

(1) UNIVERSITALY PRE-ENROLMENT — compulsory and the visa prerequisite: "JUNE – 15 – 2026 – Pre-enrolment application deadline to University of Naples Federico II. After this date no programme changes are permitted. After this date pre-enrolment is allowed to the programmes with restricted access only." THE FINAL CLAUSE IS ADVERSE FOR THIS PROGRAMME SPECIFICALLY: because the course is OPEN ACCESS ("Libero") and not a restricted-access one, 15 June 2026 appears to be a HARD cut-off for it, with no post-deadline pre-enrolment window of the sort left open for restricted-access courses. Pre-enrolment is made exclusively at https://www.universitaly.it/studenti-stranieri, indicating the University of Naples Federico II, this degree programme, and the Embassy/Consulate where the study visa will be requested.

(2) VISA: "NOVEMBER – 30 – 2026 – Deadline for submitting the Visa Application at Italian Embassies/Consulates."

(3) THE PROGRAMME'S OWN ADMISSION PROCESS — PUBLICLY DECLARED NOT YET OPEN, AND NEVER SUBSEQUENTLY UPDATED. The department published a notice dated 2 March 2026, signed by the course coordinator, addressed specifically to non-EU candidates for this degree: "Dear non-EU candidates for the Master's Degree Programme 'Lingue e Letterature per il Plurilinguismo Europeo' (Languages and Literatures for European Plurilingualism): please note that the admissions process for the 2026/27 academic year has not yet opened. This will probably happen in March. Consequently, we are unable to evaluate candidates' eligibility or send pre-acceptance letters. You can always find the latest information about opening dates at https://www.international.unina.it/education/admission-regulation/. Please contact us at the following mail address: international.ma.plurilingualism@gmail.com as soon as the application process is available. Prof. Luca Zenobi (Coordinator of the MA Degree Programme)". No follow-up notice announcing the opening was ever posted: the course's notice board shows only three items after that date — a translation summer school (17 March 2026) and the 2026/2027 teaching calendar (29 May 2026) — and no admission announcement at all.

EXPLICIT OFFICIAL CAVEATS: "Be aware that pre-enrolment alone does not grant admission to degree programmes. In order to matriculate you also need to take and pass the verifications of the entry requirements and the admission procedures set for the degree programme of your interest." And: "Important! The University of Naples Federico II does not issue admission letters for obtaining a visa." — consistent with the coordinator's statement that no pre-acceptance letters could be sent.

NON-EU CANDIDATES WHO DO NOT NEED A VISA (legally resident in Italy or an EU country) are exempt from Universitaly entirely: "Non-European candidates, wherever they reside and regularly residing in Italy or in a European Union country, have unrestricted access to university courses if they hold a qualification corresponding to the required Italian qualification... You will therefore not need to pre-register on the Universitaly Portal." They present academic documents directly to the Course Coordinator, like EU candidates.

Marked uncertain because the programme-level process was still closed at its last public update, its opening was never announced, and no unina.it page reconciles a course whose own admission process opened (at best) in or after March with a hard 15 June Universitaly cut-off. A candidate abroad must treat 2026-06-15 as the binding practical deadline for 2026/27 and, at this date, should write to international.ma.plurilingualism@gmail.com about the 2027/28 cycle instead.
required_documents:
[uncertain] NO CONSOLIDATED PROGRAMME-SPECIFIC DOCUMENT CHECKLIST IS PUBLISHED for this course — there is no application form, no downloadable module and no document list on the departmental course pages, in marked contrast to other Federico II master's programmes. The list below is assembled from the University's central rules, which are the only applicable published sources.

FOR ASSESSMENT OF A FOREIGN QUALIFICATION (EU and non-EU alike), sent to the Course Coordinator: "– eventual translations – legalisations – Diploma Supplement – certificates of examinations – certificates from the Italian ENICNARIC centre (CIMEA) https://www.cimea.it/EN/ – any declarations of value issued by the competent diplomatic representations". Because of this programme's 48+48 CFU rule, a COMPLETE TRANSCRIPT OF RECORDS SHOWING PER-MODULE CREDIT VOLUMES IN FOREIGN LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES is in practice the critical document, since the CCD must map it onto the L-LIN/xx sectors; module syllabi should be expected to be requested as well, the regulations providing that the CCD proceeds by "analysis of the activities carried out" and "evaluation of the congruity of the disciplinary scientific sectors and of the contents of the training activities".

FOR NON-EU CANDIDATES AT THE EMBASSY: "the summary of the pre-enrolment application submitted through Universitaly and validated by the University of Naples Federico II; any language competence certificates (see information on how to meet the Italian language requirement); the documents required for the visa application, including a health insurance policy where applicable; the required documents if you hold a foreign qualification." Visa material requirements: proof of means of subsistence of €10,179.85 per year, funds for repatriation, suitable accommodation in Italy, and adequate medical/hospitalisation insurance valid in Italy.

FOR ENROLMENT (matriculation), per the central regulation: "Copy of passport; Application form; 1 passport photo; Tax code [codice fiscale]; Residence permit (proof of having applied for it); Declaration of value issued by the Italian Embassy in the country where the degree was obtained or certificate of validity issued by ENIC-NARIC centres." Matriculation is transacted through the University's SegrePass portal (https://www.segrepass1.unina.it/Welcome.do), which the orientation portal links as "ACCESS THE REGISTRATION PORTAL".

LIKELY ADDITIONAL, GIVEN THIS PROGRAMME'S RULES BUT NOT PUBLISHED AS A REQUIREMENT: evidence of Italian proficiency at B2 for foreign-degree holders (Art. 4 §2 leaves the evidence standard to the CCD, naming no certificate), and an English certificate for the visa file.

The central page carries the standing warning: "Important: always check the instructions on the degree programme's website" — which for this course currently publishes nothing. Marked uncertain on that basis: the checklist above is the University's generic one, not a course-specific one, and the CCD may request more.
entry_exam_or_test:
[uncertain] THERE IS NO STANDING ENTRANCE EXAMINATION, BUT THE COMMISSION MAY IMPOSE ONE. No TOLC, no SAT, no multiple-choice test, no GRE/GMAT and no scheduled admission examination is published for this programme anywhere on unina.it. Admission is "Libero" (open access).

What exists instead is a DISCRETIONARY, RESERVED POWER, stated twice in the didactic regulations in identical terms — once in Art. 4 (admission requirements) and again in Art. 5 (procedures for access): "The Commission for the Didactic Coordination of the Master's Degree Course assesses on a case-by-case basis the adequacy of the personal preparation of the applicants whose applications have been received. It reserves the right to carry out written tests and personal interviews, also through special committees." The departmental course page repeats the Italian original: "Accanto al possesso degli specifici requisiti curriculari, l'ammissione al CdSM è subordinata alla verifica dell'adeguatezza della personale preparazione dello studente... Essa si riserva la facoltà di effettuare dei test scritti e dei colloqui personali, anche attraverso apposite commissioni."

SO THE CORRECT MODEL IS: a documentary eligibility check (degree class + 48+48 CFU) is mandatory for everyone; a written test and/or personal interview is OPTIONAL AT THE COMMISSION'S DISCRETION and may be convened for any applicant — most plausibly for foreign-degree holders, whose credits and Italian proficiency the regulations elsewhere direct the CCD to assess individually. No dates, venue, format, syllabus, score scale, weighting or ranking procedure is published for any such test, and none needs to be, because the course is uncapped and the assessment is a pass/suitability gate rather than a ranked competition.

DISTINGUISH THE IN-COURSE SELECTIONS, WHICH ARE REAL AND COMPETITIVE BUT ARE NOT ADMISSION TESTS. For the Osnabrück binational track: "participants in the programme are selected through an interview conducted by their respective institution. If the number of applications exceeds the number of places available, a ranking is drawn up on the basis of merit criteria (degree mark, average marks, number of exams taken). In the event of a tied score, the candidate with the highest average mark in the examinations in German studies takes precedence, then the candidate with the highest overall average mark, and finally the candidate with the highest Bachelor's degree mark." For Bordeaux-Montaigne: "Students who wish to participate in the exchange program are selected on the basis of their academic results (degree grade, average of exams taken, number of exams taken)." Both selections are "carried out by the Commission for the Coordination of the Master's Degree Course during the first year of studies" — i.e. they concern students already enrolled.

Marked uncertain because whether a test or interview is actually convened is entirely at the CCD's discretion and is nowhere documented for any past cycle; an international applicant cannot know in advance whether they will face one, nor prepare for it.
seats_total:
[uncertain] NO SEAT CAP IS PUBLISHED, and the best reading of the official record is that none exists for admission. The orientation portal header records "Admission Libero" (open/free access); the departmental record gives "Accesso al Corso: Laurea di 1° livello" with no numerical quota. The course is not listed among Federico II's "corsi a numero programmato" and has no rectoral admission decree setting places. Under Italian law an uncapped Laurea Magistrale admits all candidates who satisfy the curricular requirements and pass the personal-preparation check, so a "total seats" figure is conceptually absent rather than merely unpublished.

THE ONLY NUMBERS PUBLISHED ANYWHERE IN THIS COURSE'S DOCUMENTS ARE THE BINATIONAL-TRACK PLACES, AND THEY MUST NOT BE MISTAKEN FOR AN ADMISSION QUOTA. Osnabrück track: "The number of students from each institution who can access the programme annually is five." Bordeaux-Montaigne track: "Each institution will host a maximum number of 5 (five) students per academic year from the partner University." These are caps on outbound mobility places within the double-degree agreements, allocated by ranked selection among students ALREADY ENROLLED, during their first year — they do not limit entry to the degree.

Marked uncertain because this is an inference from the "Libero" tag plus the absence of any quota, not from an explicit statement that places are unlimited, which no unina.it page makes for this programme. No cohort-size or enrolment-numbers figure is published on unina.it either.
non_eu_reserved_seats:
[uncertain] NO NON-EU RESERVED QUOTA IS PUBLISHED for this programme on any unina.it page. This follows from seats_total: an open-access ("Libero") course has no seat pool to subdivide, so no "posti riservati agli studenti extracomunitari" figure of the kind published for capped courses appears in this course's record. Consistent with this, the University's central admission regulation reserves post-deadline Universitaly pre-enrolment for "the programmes with restricted access only", implicitly classing this course outside the restricted-access/quota regime, and the central page's discussion of reserved access and admission-test rankings is framed around "First-cycle and single-cycle degree courses", not master's courses.

The international dimension is instead handled qualitatively and individually: the CCD evaluates "enrolment received from students holding degrees obtained at foreign universities" case by case, assesses their Italian proficiency case by case, and — per the coordinator's own notice — issues no pre-acceptance letters ("we are unable to evaluate candidates' eligibility or send pre-acceptance letters" while the process is closed).

Marked uncertain because the annual ministerial/rectoral document that assigns non-EU visa contingents across Federico II's degree programmes was not located on unina.it during this research, so the existence of an administrative non-EU contingent at University level (as distinct from a programme-level reserved-seat quota) cannot be excluded.

(1) The international.unina.it admission regulation prints flat figures: "Fees – Eropean students €200/year (tuition fees) + €140/year regional tax (compulsory) + €16.00 legal stamp (compulsory) – Non-european students €140/year regional fee (compulsory) + €16.00 legal stamp (compulsory)" [sic, 'Eropean']. Read literally this implies non-EU students pay no tuition component at all, only the €140 regional tax and €16 stamp — an unusually favourable reading that should be confirmed before being relied upon. (2) The main fee pages publish no figures and route students to the ISEE-based calculator, consistent with Federico II's standard income-assessed student-contribution system (fixed component + regional tax + ISEE-scaled variable contribution, with a "no-tax area" exemption at low ISEE brackets and exemptions for students with recognised disability). NO PROGRAMME-SPECIFIC TUITION FIGURE EXISTS for this course, and neither the departmental course pages nor the orientation portal sheet mentions fees at all. Bracket amounts change annually and must be taken from the calculator or the current fee regulation. Note separately that the visa route requires proof of means of subsistence of €10,179.85 per year, which dominates the fee amounts in practice for a non-EU applicant. Scholarship note: the only financial support named in this course's own documents is Erasmus funding for the binational tracks — "Scholarships made available by the University through the Erasmus Office are available for selected UNINA students" — which is mobility funding for enrolled students, not an entry scholarship.

uncertainty_notes:
1) CAMPUS RESOLVED. The research brief listed campus as "to be verified". It is confirmed as Naples HISTORIC CENTRE — the Department of Humanities sites, primarily Complesso di San Pietro Martire, Via Porta di Massa 1, 80133 Napoli, with three further published buildings (Via Marina 33; Corso Umberto I 40; Via Mezzocannone 16). This is NOT Monte Sant'Angelo (where the science, engineering and economics courses sit), nor Policlinico, Portici, San Giovanni a Teduccio or Frullone. The Student Registry Office is at a different address again (Via Giulio Cesare Cortese 29) and should not be mistaken for the teaching venue.

2) THE "ENG" TAG IS THE BIGGEST INTERPRETIVE TRAP IN THIS RECORD — HIGHEST-IMPACT CAVEAT. The orientation portal header and the international catalogue both tag this course "ENG", the identical marker used for Federico II's genuinely English-medium degrees such as LMEF, Data Science or Quantum Science and Engineering. But the binding regulations describe something different: students have "the possibility... to carry out their entire course of study in English or, for the other foreign languages and literatures, in the relevant languages and in English". English is an available complete route through a course that is by design taught across French, Spanish, English, German and Italian — it is the mechanism by which the course qualifies as "international" under M.D. 6/2019, not a statement that all teaching is in English. Published study plans include unavoidably Italian-medium modules (Italian Linguistics is compulsory in the Linguistic curriculum; Italian literature, Latin, pedagogy and psychology modules recur as options), the regulations are published in Italian, English, French and German, the thesis may be written in Italian or any studied foreign language with part of the defence in a foreign language, and the Bordeaux double degree under this same course is catalogued "ITA/FRA" with no English at all. NO unina.it source gives a module-by-module language map or guarantees that an English-only path is timetabled in any given year. Treat this as a plurilingual course with an English option, not as an English-taught degree.

3) ITALIAN B2 IS AN EXPLICIT ENTRY REQUIREMENT IN THE COURSE'S OWN REGULATION, AND IT CONFLICTS WITH THE UNIVERSITY'S CENTRAL WAIVER — THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL BARRIER. Art. 4 §2 states: "The minimum entry level required in each language, including Italian, is B2 of the Common European Framework (CEFR)", and for foreign-degree holders the CCD "shall assess on a case-by-case basis the possession of the minimum level of knowledge of the Italian language". Meanwhile international.unina.it says B2 Italian "is not required" for a degree course in English. Two reasons not to rely on the waiver here: (a) the waiver clause enumerates "three-year, five-year or single-cycle" courses and omits magistrale (master's) courses, while the clause imposing the requirement expressly includes them — so the waiver's literal scope may not even reach this degree; (b) the waiver governs the central visa/pre-enrolment gate, whereas Art. 4 §2 is the course's own academic admission rule, and nothing on unina.it subordinates one to the other. For a non-Italian-speaking applicant this is the likeliest point of failure and must be settled in writing with the coordinator before applying.

4) THE 48+48 CFU RULE IS A SECOND, EQUALLY SEVERE BARRIER FOR FOREIGN APPLICANTS, AND ITS APPLICATION TO NON-ITALIAN DEGREES IS UNDOCUMENTED. Entry requires 48 CFU across two of four foreign-language sectors PLUS 48 CFU across two of four foreign-literature sectors — 96 CFU of a 180-CFU bachelor, in two languages, mapped to Italian L-LIN/xx sector codes that no foreign transcript carries. Unlike LMEF, whose sources state explicitly that foreign applicants' credits are "individually determined by the Master's admission committee", NO comparable relieving statement is published for this course: the regulations state the rule flatly, and the only foreign-degree carve-out mentioned anywhere concerns Italian-language assessment, not credits. Compounding this, there is no conditional/OFA route — "Students who do not meet the above-mentioned requirements may only be admitted... after having acquired the relevant credits" — so a shortfall must be made good before entry (single courses, recognisable up to 36 CFU). Whether and how a foreign languages degree satisfies the rule rests wholly on unpublished CCD judgement.

5) NO 2026/2027 ADMISSION PROCESS WAS EVER ANNOUNCED, AND THE ONLY NOTICE SAYS IT WAS CLOSED. The single programme-specific admission document on unina.it is the coordinator's notice of 2 March 2026 stating that admissions for 2026/27 "has not yet opened", that it "will probably happen in March", and that "we are unable to evaluate candidates' eligibility or send pre-acceptance letters". No opening announcement followed: the course's notice board shows only a summer school (17 March 2026) and the 2026/2027 teaching calendar (29 May 2026) after it. As of the research date (2026-08-30) there is therefore no published application window, no deadline and no application form for this programme, while the central non-EU pre-enrolment cut-off of 15 June 2026 has already passed — and, because the course is open access rather than restricted access, the central rule allows no post-deadline pre-enrolment for it. A non-EU candidate should treat 2026/27 as effectively closed and enquire about 2027/28.

6) NO PROGRAMME-SPECIFIC DOCUMENT CHECKLIST, APPLICATION FORM OR FIRST-YEAR DEADLINE EXISTS. Unlike LMEF (which publishes a downloadable application form and a dated interview notice), this course publishes none. The only enrolment window on the orientation sheet — 1 September to 31 October — is expressly stated to concern "years following the first one", so it does not even establish the first-year window. required_documents above is therefore assembled from the University's generic central rules.

7) INTERNAL COURSE-CODE DISCREPANCY: P60 vs P61. The official didactic regulations are headed and filed as P60 ("P60 DSU Regulation CdSM Languages and Literatures for European Multilingualism"; file names P60_RegolamentoDidattico...), and the departmental detail record also prints "(P60)". But the department's main course landing page prints "(P61)". P60 is the better-evidenced code. This affects nothing substantive but may matter when quoting a code in correspondence.

8) CURRICULA COUNT AND DOUBLE-DEGREE PARTNERS ARE INCONSISTENT ACROSS OFFICIAL PAGES. The orientation portal and the regulations say FOUR curricula and omit the Binational Linguistic "Didattica del FLE"; the departmental detail record says FIVE and includes it. On partners: the regulations (Art. 1 §4) name only Osnabrück (joint degree) and Bordeaux-Montaigne (double degree); the orientation portal's double-degree paragraph names Bordeaux (UBM) and Paris-Est Créteil (UPEC) but not Osnabrück; the contacts list names referents for all THREE (Bongo/Osnabrück, Puolato/Bordeaux-Montaigne, Lo Feudo/UPEC). Best reconciliation: three partner universities exist, with UPEC the most recent addition not yet folded into the 2022/23 regulations, and each page reflects a different vintage. Anyone targeting a specific binational track must confirm it is currently active.

9) OFFICIAL ENGLISH NAME IS UNSTABLE — "PLURILINGUALISM" vs "MULTILINGUALISM". Both appear in official University text, sometimes on the same page: the regulations' cover reads "PLURILINGUALISM" while their own footer reads "Multilingualism", and the orientation portal switches forms between paragraphs. The Italian legal title ("Lingue e Letterature per il Plurilinguismo Europeo") is stable and is what appears on the diploma; "Plurilingualism" is used here as the official English rendering because it is the form in the page titles, the international catalogue and the URL. The regulations' cover also contains the typo "PLURILINGUSLISM".

10) WORDING DEFECT IN THE ADMISSION RULE ("as well as" vs "or"). The English regulations link the two lists of admissible bachelor's classes with "as well as", which read literally would require degrees under both Ministerial Decree 509/1999 and Ministerial Decree 270/2004 simultaneously — impossible, as these are successive versions of the same framework. The orientation portal's "or in one of the following classes" is the intended meaning, and the same "as well as" construction is separately (and correctly) used to join the two 48-CFU blocks, where it genuinely does mean "in addition to". Quoted verbatim above so the ambiguity is visible.

11) SEATS AND NON-EU QUOTA ARE ABSENT BY DESIGN, NOT MERELY UNFOUND — BUT THIS IS AN INFERENCE. No admission seat total and no non-EU reserved-seat figure is published, the expected state for an "accesso libero" course with no bando. However, no unina.it page affirmatively states that places are unlimited, and the University-level document assigning non-EU visa contingents across programmes was not located, so a University-level administrative contingent cannot be strictly excluded. Do not mistake the "five students per institution per year" figures in the regulations' annexes for admission places: those cap the Osnabrück and Bordeaux mobility tracks and are allocated by ranked selection among students already enrolled, during the first year.

12) THE REGULATIONS ARE DATED. The governing didactic regulations have been "in force since the academic year 2022-2023" and were last re-uploaded in January 2025; internal references run to a Department Council meeting of 13.12.2023. The orientation portal sheet, by contrast, is marked "Updated 2026/2027". Where the two diverge (curricula count, double-degree partners) the orientation portal is more current, but the regulations remain the binding instrument on admission requirements. No newer edition is published on the course's regulations page.

13) THE DEDICATED INTERNATIONAL CONTACT IS A GMAIL ADDRESS. The department directs prospective international applicants to international.ma.plurilingualism@gmail.com — not an @unina.it address. It is published on the official departmental notice over the coordinator's name, so it is authentic, but candidates should expect to corroborate anything material against the coordinator's institutional address (luca.zenobi@unina.it).

14) NO ENTRY SCHOLARSHIP SCHEME IS PUBLISHED for this course. The only financial support named in its own documents is Erasmus funding for students selected onto the binational tracks — mobility money for enrolled students, not admission scholarships. The University-wide scholarship page is https://www.unina.it/en/ateneo/concorsi-e-borse-di-studio/borse-di-studio.

15) TECHNICAL NOTE ON SOURCING. orientamento.unina.it and studiumanistici.unina.it present TLS certificate-chain errors to standard fetchers ("unable to verify the first certificate") and had to be retrieved with a direct HTTP client; the departmental notice-board index path /avvisi/bacheca-studenti/ returns a 404 while the per-course category path works. These are site-infrastructure issues, not content problems, but they mean some unina.it material may be unreachable to automated checks and should be re-verified manually near an application deadline. All content in this record was taken from unina.it domains only (orientamento.unina.it, studiumanistici.unina.it, international.unina.it); no third-party aggregator was used as a source for any field value.
